PSBP-00001.teaser: A single bulb beneath this plant can weigh forty pounds — one of the largest in the plant kingdom. Its white flowers open at dusk, timed to hawk moths.

PSBP-00002.teaser: That red bottlebrush is not made of petals — it is a burst of pollen-bearing stamens. Crush a leaf and it smells of citrus.

PSBP-00003.teaser: Fewer than fifty survive in the wild in Florida, all on Elliott Key. Every one growing in cultivation is a conservation choice somebody made.

PSBP-00004.teaser: The conical spines on this trunk are thought to be armor against giant ground sloths and gomphotheres — South American megafauna long since extinct.

PSBP-00005.teaser: Each flower runs a quiet con: it offers bees a generous helping of dummy pollen as a food reward, while keeping the real fertile pollen hidden nearby.

PSBP-00006.teaser: A game while you are here: find three different leaf shapes on one branch — oval, fiddle, and three-lobed all grow at once. Every part of it is poisonous.

PSBP-00007.teaser: When it blooms the entire canopy turns purple-blue before a single leaf appears — one of the most theatrical flowering displays in the botanical world.

PSBP-00008.teaser: It grows where almost nothing else will, on bare coastal dune, and its seeds feed songbirds migrating down the Gulf Coast every fall.

PSBP-00009.teaser: Celebrated for generations as a Florida native, until a 2020 genetic study placed its origin in the Great Plains. Bees and butterflies treat it as native regardless.

PSBP-00010.teaser: Audubon painted his White-crowned Pigeon sitting in one of these during his 1832 Florida expedition — the picture put both bird and tree on the map.

PSBP-00011.teaser: It can live a thousand years and hold tens of thousands of gallons of water in its trunk. In drought, elephants tear the trunks open to get at it.

PSBP-00012.teaser: Linnaeus thought it so beautiful he named it pulcherrima — Latin for 'most beautiful.' It is the national flower of Barbados.

PSBP-00013.teaser: Touch the leaves and they fold shut in seconds — a defense that confuses insects and startles nearly everyone who walks past.

PSBP-00014.teaser: What looks like a two-toned flower is two structures: the true petals drop early, but the star-shaped calyx holds on, leaving a lavender haze for weeks.

PSBP-00016.teaser: The leaves do what flowers usually do — they are the show, and they burn brighter the more sun they get.

PSBP-00017.teaser: Unlike almost every other palm, it suckers from the base. Plant one and it slowly becomes a grove without you ever planting a second.

PSBP-00018.teaser: Florida calls it the Tourist Tree, because the bark is always red and peeling. Cut a branch, stick it in the ground, and it roots — the Seminoles built living fences.

PSBP-00019.teaser: Fewer than fifteen mature trees survive in the wild, on one small island — yet it is among the most commonly planted ornamental palms in South Florida.

PSBP-00020.teaser: The Canary Islands were named for dogs, not birds — Canariae Insulae, Islands of the Dogs. The bird was named after the islands, and this palm after both.

PSBP-00021.teaser: In Madagascar it is pollinated by lemurs, which push their faces into the flowers and carry the pollen away on their snouts.

PSBP-00022.teaser: It contains bilirubin — a pigment otherwise found in animals, made when red blood cells break down. One of the very few plants confirmed to produce it.

PSBP-00023.teaser: The oldest known Bald Cypress is 2,624 years old, the oldest living tree in eastern North America. This one drops every needle each fall; few conifers do.

PSBP-00024.teaser: Nabisco once ground twenty tons of coontie root a day into animal crackers, until the FDA banned it in 1925. It is also the sole host of the Atala butterfly.

PSBP-00025.teaser: Its berries ferment on the branch. Cedar Waxwings that gorge on them have been documented flying drunk — and colliding with windows.

PSBP-00026.teaser: Every October it throws up a cloud of pink seed plumes so fine they seem to float — the reason it now lines miles of Florida highway median.

PSBP-00027.teaser: British cannonballs bounced off the Live Oak hull of the USS Constitution in 1812. That is how she earned the name Old Ironsides.

PSBP-00028.teaser: Its seeds germinate while still on the tree, then drop into the water as foot-long seedlings that can float for a year and cross an ocean before rooting.

PSBP-00029.teaser: The name is literal. When an alligator moves through a stand of it, the tall leaves wave along its path — and trackers read the flag.

PSBP-00030.teaser: It is a close enough relative of corn that the two can hybridize — and its seed spike looks like a miniature ear. The popped seeds taste like popcorn.

PSBP-00031.teaser: Dutch elm disease erased the arching canopies that once lined American streets coast to coast. Florida's own variety still stands in floodplain forests.

PSBP-00032.teaser: Spanish shipbuilders chose this wood for hulls that shrugged off cannon fire and shipworm, centuries before Chippendale made it the furniture of Georgian England.

PSBP-00033.teaser: Small, thorny, easy to overlook — and the essential host plant for the Giant Swallowtail, Florida's largest butterfly, with a six-inch wingspan.

PSBP-00034.teaser: Its seeds are so hard they have been found intact — and still able to sprout — in pre-Columbian archaeological sites.

PSBP-00035.teaser: That smooth green column below the fronds is not trunk. It is a crownshaft of wrapped leaf bases, and the palm sheds it whole when it self-cleans.

PSBP-00036.teaser: Look closely at a flower: the top petal is splashed yellow and white, a landing strip aimed at pollinators. In bloom the whole canopy goes vermillion.

PSBP-00037.teaser: Birds eat the red berries and drop the seeds high in native trees, where a seedling can take root in the canopy and slowly strangle its host.

PSBP-00038.teaser: Its seed capsules are spring-loaded: when rain wets them they catapult seed several feet. That, plus underground runners, is why it is a Category I invasive.

PSBP-00039.teaser: Monarch and Queen caterpillars do not just eat this plant — they absorb its cardiac toxins and carry that chemical armor into adulthood, poisonous to birds.

PSBP-00040.teaser: It spends ten to thirty years saving up for one bloom. The stalk then rockets up a foot a day to twenty feet — and the whole plant dies, having flowered once.

PSBP-00041.teaser: The seeds are so hard and round they were once loaded into shotguns as improvised pellets — which is how the plant earned its old name, Indian Shot.

PSBP-00042.teaser: The flower spike coils like a scorpion's tail and uncurls slowly, opening one tiny white bloom at a time from base to tip.

PSBP-00043.teaser: This genus grows wild in only two places on Earth: a strip of South African coast, and one island in the Tasman Sea 9,000 miles away. Nobody knows how it crossed.

PSBP-00044.teaser: No pine at all — it is closer to grasses and orchids than to any conifer. It walks on stilt roots, and its leaves spiral up the trunk like a screw thread.

PSBP-00045.teaser: Touch a spent bloom and it sticks. Glandular hairs at the flower base hitch a ride on fur and clothing, carrying the seed somewhere new.

PSBP-00046.teaser: The famously indestructible houseplant, surviving shade, drought and neglect. In 2017 DNA evidence moved it out of Sansevieria into the dragon-tree genus.

PSBP-00047.teaser: It grows two kinds of leaf: flat brown shields that grip the host and catch falling debris for compost, and arching antlers that do the photosynthesis.

PSBP-00048.teaser: The deep lobes let storm wind pass straight through the leaf instead of tearing it — an adaptation to the violent afternoon storms of its home forests.

PSBP-00049.teaser: That white flag is not a petal but a modified leaf, wrapped around a spike of tiny true flowers. In the wild the spike warms at night to draw in beetles.

PSBP-00051.teaser: Each flower holds roughly four hundred stamens. The Aztecs called it Cornsilk Flower; the Spanish called it Angel Hair. Both were describing the same thing.

PSBP-00052.teaser: It flowers through autumn and winter, timed to the Monarch migration down the peninsula. Fifty or more butterflies have been counted on a single vine at peak.

PSBP-00053.teaser: Pentas is Greek for five, and the plant keeps its word — five petals, five sepals, five stamens on every flower, without exception.

PSBP-00054.teaser: Leaves reach three feet across, big enough to hold over your head in rain, which is why it is also called Eve's Umbrella. Young plants grow the largest ones.

PSBP-00055.teaser: The specimen that first gave this plant its scientific name was collected on Tampa Bay in the 1840s by an Army surgeon named Hulse. It still carries his name.

PSBP-00056.teaser: The curved bract is a near-exact match for a hummingbird's bill. In its home range, hummingbirds claim individual plants and defend them as private nectar bars.

PSBP-00057.teaser: Colonial Americans boiled the wax off these berries to make bayberry candles — cleaner-burning than tallow, better smelling, and still sold today.

PSBP-00058.teaser: Fronds reach twelve feet — the largest fern in the state, and among all fifty states it grows wild only here. Cold is what keeps it on the peninsula.

PSBP-00059.teaser: Crush a leaf and rub it on your arms. The compound it releases repels mosquitoes about as well as DEET — folk knowledge the laboratory later confirmed.

PSBP-00060.teaser: Sacred to the Maya as the World Tree: roots in the underworld, trunk in ours, canopy in the heavens. Hurricane Milton took its top third in 2024. It is growing back.

PSBP-00061.teaser: Each flower opens at dawn and is gone by noon. After blooming, the stem bends to the ground and roots where it lands. This is the walk in its name.

PSBP-00062.teaser: The leaves were rubbed directly on ringworm across its native range, which is why it is also called the ringworm bush. Leaves and seeds are toxic to eat.

PSBP-00064.teaser: The tube-shaped flowers are open to butterflies and hummingbirds and closed to almost everything else — only long mouthparts can reach the nectar.

PSBP-00065.teaser: Not bamboo, and not related to it. Its berries carry cyanide compounds, tolerable in small amounts, but they have killed Cedar Waxwings that gorged on them.

PSBP-00066.teaser: Its starchy tubers — duck potatoes — were a staple food across the Southeast and were traded widely. Ducks and muskrats dig them up too.

PSBP-00067.teaser: This small bedding plant is the source of vincristine and vinblastine, chemotherapy drugs still used against childhood leukemia and Hodgkin's lymphoma.

PSBP-00068.teaser: A fig is not a fruit but a hollow chamber lined with flowers, pollinated by a single species of wasp that crawls in through a pinhole and dies inside.

PSBP-00069.teaser: In the scrub it evolved for, fire burns the whole plant to the ground — and new shoots push up from the surviving roots within weeks.

PSBP-00070.teaser: The flower is not the show. What follows it is: a waxy red-purple calyx that swells and holds for weeks while the fruit ripens inside.

PSBP-00071.teaser: A stem cutting left on damp soil will root. Hawaiian voyagers carried ti stems on long ocean crossings and planted them at every new landfall.

PSBP-00072.teaser: Across Latin America it is called esperanza — hope. It is the national flower of the Bahamas and the official flower of the US Virgin Islands.

PSBP-00073.teaser: Nearly all of its hundred-odd Thunbergia relatives are aggressive climbers. This one stayed a shrub, which is the only reason it is welcome in a garden.

PSBP-00074.teaser: It flowers and fruits at the same time, all year — which is why hummingbirds, butterflies and more than two dozen bird species work it in every season.

PSBP-00075.teaser: Give the flower a sniff — most people get old lemon furniture polish. That is deliberate: the smell is bait for the flies that pollinate it.

PSBP-00076.teaser: It was collected at Rio in 1767 by Jeanne Baret, who joined the voyage disguised as a man. The plant was named for her commander, who stayed with the ships.

PSBP-00078.teaser: Unlike the tropical milkweed sold in most nurseries, this one dies back each season — the cue that tells Monarchs to keep migrating instead of staying put.

PSBP-00079.teaser: Not a tree at all — the trunk is soft and pithy, with no wood in it. A papaya grown from seed can be carrying fruit in under a year.

PSBP-00080.teaser: The flower opens once, after dark, up to a foot across, then closes by morning. Bats and moths pollinate it while the park is asleep.

PSBP-00081.teaser: Not a moss and not a parasite — it is a bromeliad, a cousin of the pineapple. It takes water and food from the air; the tree provides only a perch.

PSBP-00082.teaser: The leaflets look like torn paper, or a fish's tail. Each trunk fruits exactly once and then dies, while the clump carries on from new stems at the base.

PSBP-00083.teaser: No palm at all. It is a succulent with a fat, water-storing trunk, more closely related to milkweed and oleander than to anything in the palm family.

PSBP-00084.teaser: Its trunks lean outward from the base instead of standing straight, growing in clumps along African rivers — the reclining habit that named it.

PSBP-00085.teaser: One of the most shade-tolerant palms in cultivation. It grows under closed forest canopy, which makes it the answer for deep shade beneath a Live Oak.

PSBP-00086.teaser: Gram for gram the leaves carry more vitamin C than oranges, more calcium than milk, more iron than spinach and more potassium than bananas.

PSBP-00087.teaser: The flowers produce no nectar at all. Sphinx moths come for the fragrance, carry pollen between plants and get nothing — pollination by deceit.

PSBP-00088.teaser: The name comes from a Caribbean brew: the leaves were boiled and fermented into a dark, foaming drink that looked enough like Porter ale for it to stick.

PSBP-00089.teaser: Nicker is an old dialect word for a marble. The seeds are perfectly round, slate-gray and nearly indestructible — and they float well enough to cross oceans.

PSBP-00090.teaser: It belongs to the cashew family, alongside poison ivy and sumac. The sap and skin carry related compounds, which is why some people react to handling it.

PSBP-00091.teaser: There are no petals — those pink puffs are made entirely of stamens. Watch near dusk and the paired leaflets fold together to sleep, reopening at dawn.

PSBP-00092.teaser: The purple is anthocyanin, a built-in sunblock against UV, and it deepens the more direct sun the plant takes. A shaded one never colors up the same way.

PSBP-00093.teaser: The color is not flower but bract — papery modified leaves. The true flowers are the small cream tubes at the center, and they do all the actual biology.

PSBP-00094.teaser: The flowers make one of the most vivid natural blue dyes known. Brewed as tea it comes out brilliant blue — and turns pink the moment you add lemon.

PSBP-00095.teaser: The name is a precise description: small white flowers sit nestled inside boat-shaped purple bracts, like a figure asleep in a cradle.

PSBP-00096.teaser: A single cherry carries roughly sixty-five times the vitamin C of an orange the same size. You never see them in supermarkets because they spoil within days.

PSBP-00097.teaser: It opens as the light fades, when most flowering shrubs have shut for the day — white stars with long purple stamens, and a scent that carries at dusk.

PSBP-00098.teaser: The seed pods pinch tight between each seed, so a finished pod hangs like a string of beads. That is the necklace the name refers to.

PSBP-00099.teaser: A soaking rain after a dry spell sets it off: the whole planting flowers within days, then goes quiet again until the next storm.

PSBP-00100.teaser: The dry pods rattle in the wind, which is where the name comes from. The toxin inside causes irreversible liver damage in horses — walkabout disease.

PSBP-00101.teaser: The clusters shade from yellow to red as each flower ages, and it is a signal: yellow is fresh and full of nectar, red is spent. Watch a butterfly skip the red.

PSBP-00102.teaser: It flowers in late winter on completely bare branches, so the red blooms have the whole tree to themselves with no leaves to compete.

PSBP-00104.teaser: Early Florida pioneers roasted the berries as a coffee substitute and gave it up quickly — the drink was bitter and brought on severe headaches.

PSBP-00107.teaser: This is the plant our volunteers fight hardest. It has reached nearly every corner of the park, and we pull it entirely by hand, one runner at a time.

PSBP-00108.teaser: Dismissed as a lawn weed, and called Florida snow for the way the blooms can whiten a lawn overnight. Bees and butterflies work it hard regardless.

PSBP-00109.teaser: A true orchid, growing in the turf. It has adapted to the mower: it can throw up a spike, get pollinated and drop seed inside the week between cuts.

PSBP-00110.teaser: As the pods dry they inflate like small balloons, and the loose seeds inside turn the whole plant into a maraca. A delightful sound for something so toxic.

PSBP-00112.teaser: Each leaf is split at the tip into two matching lobes. The genus honors the Bauhin brothers, twin botanists — the paired leaf is the joke, and it is deliberate.

PSBP-00113.teaser: A native mat low enough to be mown and walked on without complaint, and its pinhead flowers feed small native bees that larger blooms shut out.

PSBP-00116.teaser: One of the last native plants still flowering in November, when almost nothing else is — which makes it critical fuel for monarchs heading south.

PSBP-00117.teaser: Goldenrod takes the blame for autumn hay fever it does not cause. Its pollen is heavy and insect-carried. The real culprit is ragweed, blooming alongside.

PSBP-00118.teaser: The coral-red tubular flowers bring in hummingbirds, and the star-shaped seed capsules that follow are nearly as ornamental as the flowers were.

PSBP-00119.teaser: Planted across Florida for decades as the ideal hedge, before anyone understood that birds were carrying its berries out into wild hammocks.

PSBP-00120.teaser: In the wild it is a plain green shrub. Every color you see here — red, orange, yellow, purple, often in one leaf — came from centuries of deliberate selection.

PSBP-00121.teaser: Handed down through the Baden family since the 1880s — the most historically precious plant in the park, kept alive by bulb division for a century and a half.

PSBP-00122.teaser: Look closely at a flower cluster and catch it running a con: the big showy blooms around the rim are sterile advertising, while tiny fertile flowers do the work.

PSBP-00123.teaser: The word grenade comes from this fruit. Early grenades were named for the pomegranate they resembled, packed seeds and all.

PSBP-00124.teaser: Slice it crosswise and every piece is a perfect five-pointed star. It also carries a neurotoxin that healthy kidneys filter out — and impaired ones cannot.

PSBP-00125.teaser: The hanging pods reach two feet, each divided inside into dozens of sealed chambers holding one seed apiece in sticky pulp — a very effective laxative.

PSBP-00126.teaser: Peel one and it looks startlingly like an eye — translucent flesh around a glossy black seed. That is exactly what the Cantonese name means: dragon eye.

PSBP-00127.teaser: Ripe, it looks like a green tomato and scoops out like chocolate pudding. There is no chocolate in it — the flavor and texture are entirely the fruit's own.

PSBP-00128.teaser: Also called alligator apple, after the gators that share its swamps and eat the fallen fruit. The fruit floats, so the tree plants itself downstream.

PSBP-00129.teaser: Each flower opens as female one day and male the next, switching on a schedule so the tree cannot pollinate itself. The fruit is a single-seeded berry.

PSBP-00130.teaser: Not one fruit but dozens of separate flowers fused into a single mass. The enzyme inside actually digests protein, which is why fresh pineapple stings the tongue.

PSBP-00132.teaser: The largest fruit of any tree on Earth, over a hundred pounds. They grow straight out of the trunk rather than the twigs, because only the wood can carry them.

PSBP-00137.teaser: The bud at its center is the original swamp cabbage, a regional delicacy. Taking it kills the tree — a palm has only that one growing point.

PSBP-00146.teaser: Its flowers run two or three times the size of an ordinary jasmine, with as many as eleven narrow white lobes radiating from a reddish-purple bud.

PSBP-00148.teaser: The leaflets are so thick and leathery they genuinely feel like cardboard. It is not a palm or a fern but a cycad, a seed plant older than the dinosaurs.

PSBP-00151.teaser: The showy holiday amaryllis is not really an Amaryllis at all but a Hippeastrum — and the big bulb it grows from is the most poisonous part of the plant.

PSBP-00152.teaser: Sky-blue flower sprays and drooping clusters of golden berries appear on the plant at the same time. The berries are beautiful and seriously toxic to pets.

PSBP-00155.teaser: The white trumpet flowers give way to small fruits that look convincingly like olives. It is no relation — it is a cousin of the orange-flowered Geiger tree.

PSBP-00156.teaser: The scarlet flowers are built for one visitor: when a hummingbird probes for nectar, the stamens dab pollen right onto its head, using the bird as a flying paintbrush.

PSBP-00157.teaser: Look at the frosted silver coating on the leaves: that is the plant shedding salt. It is how it survives right at the water's edge where little else can.

PSBP-00158.teaser: A wild cousin of the goji berry, with edible red fruit. On the Texas coast the same berries are a famous autumn food for endangered whooping cranes.

PSBP-00160.teaser: At midday it turns its leaflets edge-on to the sun, cutting its exposed surface like a sailor reefing sail — which is how it survives bare beach at noon.

PSBP-00165.teaser: The name ice plant has nothing to do with cold. Water-filled cells on the leaf surface catch the light and glitter, so the whole plant looks frosted.

PSBP-00170.teaser: No rose at all, but a relative of Oleander — and the Hadza of Tanzania have long boiled its sap down into arrow poison for hunting big game.

PSBP-00181.teaser: The seeds are eighty percent oil. Hawaiians strung them on a spine and burned them one after another, so the tree served as both lamp and clock.

PSBP-00182.teaser: It has no visible trunk at all. The stem runs horizontally underground, firing fronds up out of the sand — one of very few palms that lives below grade.

PSBP-00197.teaser: Every other palm in its genus flowers white or cream. This one comes out lavender, a soft purple-pink found nowhere else in the group.

PSBP-00198.teaser: Its entire wild range is a handful of creek banks on one Queensland tableland. Watch the crown in a gust — the leaflet undersides flash silver-grey.

PSBP-00199.teaser: The lavender crownshaft deepens with age, so two trees side by side can look like different species. Its fruit is the largest of any king palm.

PSBP-00206.teaser: Its flowers bloom hidden at soil level, dull and fungus-scented — pollinated by fungus gnats tricked into mistaking them for tiny mushrooms.

PSBP-00212.teaser: That silver-blue is not pigment but a heavy coat of wax the palm secretes over every frond — sunscreen that reflects tropical UV and slows water loss.

PSBP-00215.teaser: The swollen, bottle-shaped trunk this tree is famous for takes years to form — ours is still young and slender, but give it time and it will balloon out.

PSBP-00226.teaser: Known to science only from misfiled fruit until living trees turned up in 1987. Thirty-two mature trees remain in the wild — this one is a backup copy.

PSBP-00239.teaser: The only palm native to Europe, and the most northerly wild palm on Earth — there is a native stand at Genoa, forty-four degrees north.

PSBP-00240.teaser: It makes only two or three new fronds a year, and each one unfurls bright red, burgundy to hot pink, before slowly greening over a week or two.

PSBP-00241.teaser: A Florida native that shrugs off salt spray and grows right up to the dune line. The dark plum-sized fruit is edible, and birds usually reach it before people do.

PSBP-00246.teaser: The waxy leaves hold a scratch permanently, which is why people have been carving their names into them for generations. You may find fresh signatures here.

PSBP-00251.teaser: Somewhere between sixty and a hundred and thirty of these are left in the wild, all in one corner of western Cuba. The shaggy beard insulates its trunk.

PSBP-00263.teaser: Not a palm but a cycad, and its lineage runs back 280 million years — these plants were already ancient by the time Tyrannosaurus appeared.

PSBP-00264.teaser: The entire known wild population grows on one mountain in New Caledonia and has never been found anywhere else. It takes about twenty-five years to mature.

PSBP-00265.teaser: Its whole wild range is three square miles of one coral island, with fewer than a hundred trees left. The white felted crownshaft gives it away at distance.

PSBP-00269.teaser: It shrugs off tropical storms but not a knife — taking the edible heart kills the tree, and that is what nearly finished off the wild population.

PSBP-00273.teaser: Cycads evolved long before bees or butterflies existed, so this one is still pollinated the old way — by specialized beetles that breed inside the male cones.

PSBP-00280.teaser: Science described it in 2002 from a tree in a Hawaii garden; the wild plants were found afterward. Fewer than fifteen mature palms are known in Madagascar.

PSBP-00281.teaser: The name is literal: slice the upper trunk across and the cross-section is a true triangle. The leaf bases grow in three ranks, set 120 degrees apart.

PSBP-00282.teaser: The rusty fuzz on the crownshaft is tomentum, a coat of fine hairs. About five mature trees are known in the wild — it does better in gardens than at home.

PSBP-00285.teaser: Its black fruits are eaten by lemurs, which carry the hard seeds well away from the parent tree before passing them. Lose the lemurs and the palm loses its reach.

PSBP-00286.teaser: Nearly every one of its 150-odd relatives lives in Madagascar. This one is stranded on a single Tanzanian island, where its trunks once made a football goal.

PSBP-00291.teaser: This tree is probably already in your pocket. Palm oil turns up in roughly half of all packaged supermarket goods — lipstick, ice cream, soap, instant noodles.

PSBP-00296.teaser: A young vine grows toward darkness rather than light. The darkest patch on a forest floor is the shadow of a big tree, which is exactly what it needs to climb.

PSBP-00303.teaser: Not a cactus. The ridged green columns are stems doing the work of leaves, and the milky sap inside is caustic enough to blister skin.

PSBP-00305.teaser: The seed accounts for about eighty-five percent of the fruit's weight. Everything people eat comes from a thin skin of purple pulp scraped off the outside.

PSBP-00332.teaser: The definitive Victorian parlour palm — potted Kentias lined the Palm Court of the Titanic. It grows wild on one island in the Tasman Sea and nowhere else.

PSBP-00339.teaser: Palms are not built to branch — they grow from a single tip, and losing it ends the stem. This one forks anyway, routinely, right at ground level.

PSBP-00341.teaser: The trunk bulges at the middle and tapers both ways — that is the spindle. Fewer than sixty are left wild; Florida gardens hold more than its home island.

PSBP-00343.teaser: The only caffeinated plant native to North America. Southeastern peoples brewed its leaves for centuries; the tea is sold today under its old name, yaupon.

PSBP-00350.teaser: Those colorful shrimp are not flowers but overlapping bracts. The real flowers are small white tubes that poke out from between them like a head from a shell.

PSBP-00355.teaser: The genus holds exactly three species, and nature gave one to each of the three Mascarene islands: red to Réunion, blue to Mauritius, yellow to Rodrigues.

PSBP-00362.teaser: Planted across the South for hedging, and now spreading into wild woodlands where birds drop the seeds. Handsome, useful, and a genuine problem.

PSBP-00367.teaser: It spent most of the last century filed under the name decipiens — Latin for deceiving — because it had been mistaken for a different palm entirely.

PSBP-00368.teaser: Botanists long assumed these were desert relicts. A 2012 genetic study found the seeds were carried in from the north, confirming Arrernte oral tradition.

PSBP-00383.teaser: Spineless does not mean harmless. Every pad carries glochids: hair-fine barbed bristles that detach at a touch, pierce skin instantly, and are nearly invisible.

PSBP-00404.teaser: In the wild it clings to cliff faces and steep banks along the Mekong — a long way from the manicured entryways where most people meet it.

PSBP-00411.teaser: Stress it — drought, a hard prune, a sudden move — and it releases a pungent scent from its leaf glands, somewhere between spice and over-brewed coffee.

PSBP-00418.teaser: The name is literal. Nearly every relative in its genus spreads into clumps of many trunks; this one grows exactly one, always alone.

PSBP-00419.teaser: Its name means small-fruited, and it earns it — no other palm in the genus makes berries this tiny. It stayed unknown outside New Guinea until the 1970s.

PSBP-00420.teaser: A New Guinea rainforest palm that came through a 28-degree night in St. Petersburg without so much as bronzing — cold tolerance almost nobody expects of it.

PSBP-00433.teaser: Its trunk is almost entirely underground. What looks like a cluster of leaves at ground level is the crown of a palm that has been growing downward for decades.

PSBP-00439.teaser: Its seeds die if they dry out even briefly, so they must go into soil almost the moment they are collected. That alone keeps this palm scarce in cultivation.

PSBP-00445.teaser: Individual stems can pass five hundred years, and a single clonal colony has been estimated at more than five thousand — among the oldest living things in Florida.

PSBP-00460.teaser: A single fruit cluster can top a hundred pounds and throw thousands of volunteer seedlings, which is why UF/IFAS now flags this favorite as potentially invasive.

PSBP-00462.teaser: This palm's nut makes up about ninety-five percent of the entire diet of Lear's Macaw. By 1990 fewer than sixty of those parrots were left alive.

PSBP-00470.teaser: It grows about six inches a year. A specimen twenty feet tall has been quietly at it for roughly four decades.

PSBP-00477.teaser: Shipped home from Fiji in 1864 by John Gould Veitch, twenty-five years old and already a veteran plant hunter — a relic of the Victorian age of exploration.

PSBP-00483.teaser: It cannot live on rainfall alone, so a wild grove is a map: wherever these palms stand there is water underground — a seep, a spring, or a fault-line fracture.

PSBP-00485.teaser: Unknown to science until 1978, when an Aboriginal man named Wodyeti led botanists to a single hidden population. The palm's genus name honors him.

PSBP-00497.teaser: The name has nothing to do with December. It comes from the clusters of glossy red fruit that ripen in early winter, leaving the tree looking hung with ornaments.

PSBP-00509.teaser: Its flowers keep time: the style curls upward or downward through the day, so two forms take turns acting as male and then female, and never compete.

PSBP-00520.teaser: The pesticide made from its seeds does not kill insects outright. It scrambles their hormones so they stop feeding, stop developing, and never reach adulthood.

PSBP-00543.teaser: One of the most common houseplants on Earth, and critically endangered in the wild — roughly a thousand plants remain, in one strip of Madagascar coast.

PSBP-00553.teaser: Its pigment colors the painted pages of an Aztec ritual manuscript that survives in Liverpool. The petal-like rays are sterile; the center does the work.

PSBP-00556.teaser: Beekeepers bait swarm traps with its oil because the scent mimics the pheromone scout bees use to signal a good new home. Chemically, this grass speaks bee.

PSBP-00557.teaser: Cut a stem, turn it upside down, and stand it in a glass of water. Within a couple of weeks a new plant sprouts from the bracts at what was the top.

PSBP-00561.teaser: A single vine can grow eight inches in a day and reach sixty-five feet, enough to smother a cabbage palm from the ground up. Florida's fix came from Nepal: a beetle.

PSBP-00572.teaser: The first ring species ever found in a plant: two populations circled the Caribbean in opposite directions and had diverged into distinct forms by the time they met.

PSBP-00573.teaser: It looks exactly like a cactus and is not one. Cacti come only from the Americas; this is an African euphorbia that arrived at the same shape independently.

PSBP-00574.teaser: The Instagram-famous houseplant and this tree are the same species. Kept in a pot it stays polite; put it in a Florida yard and it can top twenty-five feet.

PSBP-00588.teaser: It has never been found in the wild anywhere. DNA confirms Polynesian voyagers made it, crossing two species whose homelands sit 4,000 miles apart.

PSBP-00601.teaser: Look along the leaf edges: those are not seeds but fully formed plantlets, complete with roots, waiting to drop off and grow the moment they touch soil.

PSBP-00604.teaser: Its only wild population clings to Round Island, about a square mile of volcanic rock off Mauritius, where goats and rabbits nearly finished it off.

PSBP-00605.teaser: As the bark peels away in papery strips it bares green underneath — not lichen or disease but living, photosynthesizing tissue, briefly unmasked.

PSBP-00606.teaser: The Tang emperor Xuanzong ran a horse-relay courier system to rush fresh lychees hundreds of miles to his court. The fruit was that perishable, and that prized.

PSBP-00607.teaser: The ripe flesh has the dense, dry texture of a hard-boiled egg yolk — hence the name eggfruit — and tastes more like sweet potato pie than like any fruit you know.

PSBP-00614.teaser: Crush a frond and it smells of vanilla and sweet hay — the scent that made it a lei plant in Hawaii. Fragrant, lovely, and a Category I invasive that escaped Florida gardens.

PSBP-00616.teaser: Cheese fruit and vomit fruit are both honest nicknames. The pungent, fermented smell is a broadcast aimed squarely at the fruit bats that spread its seeds.

PSBP-00621.teaser: It is not a tree — that trunk is a column of packed leaf bases that shoots up twenty feet in a season, fruits once, then dies back while new shoots take over.

PSBP-00655.teaser: The clumping habit is engineering, not decoration: packed slender trunks flex and shed wind instead of snapping, and outer stems shelter the inner ones in cold.

PSBP-00659.teaser: Those wispy green threads are not leaves but stems. The true leaves are reduced to bracts barely two millimetres long, so the plant photosynthesizes with its stems.

PSBP-00671.teaser: The flowers open at dusk and release a heavy coconut-and-vanilla scent to bring in bats. By daylight the scent is gone and the blooms have closed again.

PSBP-00681.teaser: In Brazil's Caatinga it is one of the last nesting trees of the Spix's Macaw, extinct in the wild. The 2022 reintroduction depends on enough of them surviving.

PSBP-00682.teaser: Arab traders found it thriving in India and called it tamar hindi, Indian date. Linnaeus made that official in 1753, and the name has hidden its African origin since.

PSBP-00700.teaser: Those six-foot leaves sit on top of a staple crop: the starchy corm underneath feeds roughly four hundred million people, boiled and roasted much like a potato.

PSBP-00701.teaser: The holes are not damage. The plant makes them deliberately, killing off cells in a pattern as the leaf forms — a trick almost no other flowering plant uses.

PSBP-00703.teaser: It flowers once, after thirty to eighty years of silence, throwing up the largest flower cluster of any plant on Earth, twenty feet above the crown. Then it dies.

PSBP-00704.teaser: Every other palm on Earth has fronds either fan-shaped or divided once. Fishtail palms are the only ones whose leaves divide twice.

PSBP-00711.teaser: It carries six copies of its genome instead of the usual two, and no wild population has ever been found — meaning humans shaped it from the very beginning.

PSBP-00712.teaser: The genus honors Casimiro Gómez, an Otomi man who died fighting for Mexican independence — one of very few plant genera named for an indigenous person.

PSBP-00713.teaser: Tabebuia comes from a Tupi-Guarani phrase meaning ant wood, and it earns it: the soft-pithed twigs go hollow and ants move in to colonize and defend them.

PSBP-00714.teaser: The name is an old folk claim that burning or strewing it drove off fleas. Whether it worked is doubtful, but crush a leaf and the camphor scent is unmistakable.

PSBP-00715.teaser: Ayurvedic physicians have prescribed this creeping pond-edge herb as a memory tonic for 3,000 years. White Peacock butterflies lay their eggs on it here.

PSBP-00716.teaser: An olive straight off the tree is almost inedible, savagely bitter with oleuropein. Every olive you have ever eaten was cured, brined or fermented first.

PSBP-00717.teaser: Making palm wine from this species is a one-way transaction: harvesters fell the entire mature palm and cut a cavity into the heart of the trunk to collect it.

PSBP-00719.teaser: The wax on these leaves is armor, secreted to hold moisture while the Caatinga bakes dry for months. The same compound ends up in car polish and candy shells.

PSBP-00720.teaser: It abandons the slender silhouette every other palm agrees on. The solitary trunk reaches two feet across, near-white, and reads as carved stone rather than wood.

PSBP-00723.teaser: One shrub carries green, orange, bright red and near-black fruit all at once, each at a different stage of ripening. The darker the berry, the sweeter it is.

PSBP-00725.teaser: Often called Florida's fourth mangrove, though it isn't one. Tiny glands at the base of each leaf sweep out salt, letting it live at the tide line where little else can.

PSBP-00726.teaser: The red petals are not petals but bracts — modified leaves — the same trick the holiday Poinsettia pulls. The two are cousins in the same genus.

PSBP-00730.teaser: Each flower is a two-day beetle trap: it opens female on day one, closes at dusk to hold the beetles overnight, then reopens dusted in pollen — a trick older than bees.

PSBP-00731.teaser: Calliandra means beautiful stamens, and that is the whole show: no petals, just hundreds of thread-fine stamens. The leaflets fold shut at dusk.

PSBP-00733.teaser: One of Florida's few native cacti, and state-listed as Threatened. Its big white flowers open near midnight and close by dawn — never in bloom on a daytime visit.

PSBP-00753.teaser: Those pale oval marks spiraling up the trunk are coin spots — the clean, round scars left behind each time an old frond drops away.
